items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: Switching doors doubles your chance of the car
items.claim: Three doors, one car, two goats. Pick a door. Monty (who knows where the car is) opens a different door revealing a goat. Should you switch?
items.prompt: What's the probability of winning if you switch?

options.text: 1/3 — first guess was 1/3, opening a door doesn't change anything
2/3 — your first guess had 1/3 chance of being right, so the remaining unopened door now carries the original 2/3 probability of the OTHER two doors combined
100 percent — Monty's reveal guarantees the win

items.reveal_title: Marilyn vos Savant and a thousand wrong PhDs
items.reveal:
Vos Savant published the answer 'switch' in Parade magazine in 1990. Thousands of readers wrote in — including PhDs in mathematics — insisting she was wrong. She was right.

The key: Monty knows where the car is and always reveals a goat. Your initial choice has 1/3 probability of the car. The OTHER two doors together have 2/3 probability. Monty's reveal removes one of those two doors but doesn't change the 2/3 — it now sits entirely on the remaining unopened door.

If Monty acted randomly (sometimes revealing the car himself), switching wouldn't help — but he doesn't. His knowledge is essential.

The Monty Hall puzzle is the canonical demonstration that conditional probability defeats intuition. Run the simulation 1000 times: switching wins about 667 of them, sticking wins 333.
items.why: Probability intuition assumes 'two outcomes equally likely'. Conditional probability — conditioning on what Monty reveals — distinguishes outcomes that 'look' symmetric but aren't.

items.title: A game with infinite expected payoff that no one will pay $20 to play
items.claim: Flip a fair coin. If heads, you win 2 dollars. If tails, you flip again — heads pays 4, etc. After n tails, the next heads pays 2 to the n+1 dollars. The expected payoff is infinite. People offered the game won't pay more than 10 to 20 dollars to play.
items.prompt: Why doesn't expected value match human behaviour?

options.text: Humans value money non-linearly — losing 100 dollars hurts more than the equivalent fraction of utility of gaining 100; Bernoulli proposed logarithmic utility, giving a finite expected utility despite infinite expected dollars
The game is impossible to play

items.reveal:
The expected value: (1/2)(2) + (1/4)(4) + (1/8)(8) + ... = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinity. So by pure expected-value reasoning, any finite price for the game is a great deal.

Daniel Bernoulli (1738) noted that no rational person actually pays a large sum to play. He proposed that humans value money according to a logarithmic utility function, not linearly. Expected utility for the game with log utility is finite (about ln 2 plus a small constant), giving a reasonable price.

The St. Petersburg paradox launched expected utility theory (von Neumann, Morgenstern, 1944), behavioural economics (Kahneman, Tversky, 1979), and theories of risk aversion. It's one of the founding puzzles of decision theory.

It also exposes a deeper issue: the game has finite real-world payoff (the casino can't pay infinite money), so a more accurate model bounds the prize, giving a finite expected value of perhaps 20 dollars — close to what people actually pay.
items.why: Expected value is treated as the rational basis for decision-making. The St. Petersburg paradox shows it can be unbounded for games with bounded reasonable price — and that human utility is non-linear.
